set1.q: A 66-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptomatic right pneumothorax on his upright chest radiograph. He is otherwise stable. Which intervention is contraindicated for him?
opts: Hospitalization for monitoring and supportive care is part of managing a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, which is more life-threatening because of lost pulmonary reserve. Tell: admission is expected for him, not contraindicated.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is indicated for secondary pneumothorax because recurrence rates are high and recurrence carries greater consequences. Tell: his lung disease is an indication for surgery, while it is a contraindication to aspiration.

Correct. Underlying pulmonary disease contraindicates catheter aspiration, along with traumatic or tension pneumothorax, hemodynamic instability, recurrence, bilateral pneumothoraces and bleeding disorders. His chronic obstructive pulmonary disease makes this a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, and most of those get a chest tube instead.

Most secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are treated with chest tube insertion, which is indicated for symptoms or a persistent air leak. Tell: the tube is what replaces aspiration for him, not a procedure to avoid.

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman has a very large left pleural effusion, estimated at more than 1,000 mL on imaging, with marked dyspnea. Which inspection finding is expected?
opts: A large effusion pushes the trachea away from the involved side, not toward it; that shift appears once the fluid passes 1,000 mL. Tell: her fluid is on the left, so the shift is to the right.
Inspection over a pleural effusion shows asymmetrical thoracic expansion, the affected side moving less. Tell: a left effusion over 1,000 mL limits expansion on that side.
Small effusions, under 300 mL, produce no physical examination findings. Tell: hers is more than 1,000 mL, large enough to shift the trachea away from the effusion.

Correct. With an effusion over 1,000 mL, the trachea shifts away from the involved side, so a left effusion pushes it to the right; inspection also shows asymmetrical thoracic expansion. Small effusions under 300 mL produce no examination findings, but hers is large.

set1.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after a high-speed motor vehicle crash. He is in severe respiratory distress, with blood pressure 78/50 mm Hg and heart rate 136 beats per minute. His trachea is deviated to the left, his neck veins are distended, his right chest is hyperresonant and breath sounds are absent on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Air enters the pleural space but cannot escape, a one-way valve, causing severe ventilatory compromise and a mediastinal shift to the contralateral side. Decreased venous return and cardiac output follow, with hypotension, tracheal deviation, neck vein distention and absent breath sounds, his exact picture.
Hemothorax is blood in the pleural space, and fluid is dull to percussion. Tell: his right chest is hyperresonant, the note of air, and his trachea is pushed away from it under pressure.
ruled out by a stated finding

Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinal tissues, found as subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and a crunch with each heartbeat. Tell: his findings are a hyperresonant, silent hemithorax with shock and tracheal shift.

An open pneumothorax needs a direct wound in the chest wall that lets air in during inhalation. Tell: no chest wall wound is described, and his shock with tracheal shift marks trapped air under tension.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 25-year-old man presents with his second primary spontaneous pneumothorax on the right; the first was treated 18 months ago. He is stable. Which management best prevents further recurrence?
opts: A chest tube evacuates the space in a large symptomatic episode but leaves the pleural space open to recur. Tell: for a recurrent primary pneumothorax the plan is surgery with pleurodesis.

Correct. A recurrent primary spontaneous pneumothorax calls for surgical therapy, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis, which is the best preventive procedure. Recurrence is common, approaching 50% within three years after a first episode, and his second episode proves the risk.
Recurrent pneumothorax is on the list of contraindications to catheter aspiration. Tell: his is a second episode, and aspiration does nothing to prevent a third.
ruled out by a stated finding
Observation with oxygen fits a small first primary pneumothorax with minimal symptoms. Tell: a recurrence calls for definitive prevention, which observation does not provide.

set1.q: A 15-year-old girl has pleurodynia diagnosed during a summer outbreak at her camp, with fever, knife-like pleuritic pain and tender intercostal muscles. Her chest radiograph is normal. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Therapeutic thoracentesis removes pleural fluid to relieve dyspnea. Tell: she has no effusion to remove; pleurodynia is treated with anti-inflammatory drugs and heat.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Treatment of pleurodynia is supportive: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and application of heat to the affected muscles. The course is typically benign, though symptoms may recur a few days later, and hand hygiene limits fecal-oral spread.
A chest tube drains air or fluid from the pleural space in pneumothorax or effusion. Tell: her film is normal, and the problem is inflamed intercostal muscle, not the pleural space.
ruled out by a stated finding
Oxygen at 100% by non-rebreather mask speeds resorption of air in a small pneumothorax. Tell: there is no pleural air on her normal film; her viral myalgia gets supportive care.

set1.q: A 30-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis has had two pneumothoraces in a year. She is stable, and surgery is being planned, so her team wants the most complete picture of the size and location of the pleural air and of any blebs or bullae in the underlying lung. Which imaging test is best?
opts: The standard upright chest radiograph is the initial test, showing the visceral pleural line. Tell: it starts the workup but does not map blebs and bullae or underlying disease, which her surgical planning needs.

Lung ultrasound is a rapid bedside tool that helps in the unstable patient, with absent lung sliding marking a pneumothorax. Tell: it does not assess pneumothorax size, and she is stable enough for the more detailed test.

A lateral decubitus film shows small amounts of fluid layering against the dependent parietal pleura in a pleural effusion. Tell: it is an effusion study, and ultrasound has largely replaced even that use.

Correct. Thoracic computed tomography is the best modality for determining the presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, detects blebs and bullae and assesses underlying disease; it is the diagnostic gold standard. It is impractical only when time is critical, and she is stable.

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman in the intensive care unit has a subclavian vein catheter placed for venous access. An hour later she reports new right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, and a chest radiograph shows a visceral pleural line on the right. She has no history of lung disease or chest trauma. How is her pneumothorax classified?
opts: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax needs an underlying lung abnormality, most commonly chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Tell: she has no lung disease, and the timing ties the event to the catheter placement.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Iatrogenic pneumothorax is injury to the pleura secondary to a medical intervention, and subclavian vein catheter placement is one of the listed examples, with thoracentesis, bronchoscopy and mechanical ventilation. Her symptoms began an hour after the catheter, with no lung disease or trauma.

Traumatic pneumothorax follows blunt or penetrating trauma to the thorax, such as a gunshot or stab wound. Tell: a needle placed during a procedure makes this iatrogenic, the category for pleural injury caused by a medical intervention.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax arises with no thoracic trauma and no underlying lung abnormality, classically in tall, thin young males. Tell: hers followed a procedure, so it is not spontaneous at all.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 68-year-old man on a ventilator after a car crash cannot sit up, so a supine portable chest radiograph is taken. It shows a deep sulcus sign (a dark, deep costophrenic angle) on the left. What does this finding indicate?
opts: Correct. The deep sulcus sign is seen on a supine film: a dark and deep costophrenic angle caused by a lateral collection of pleural air. In this patient lying flat, it is how a pneumothorax shows itself.

Fluid blunts the costophrenic angle on an upright film, 75 mL the posterior angle and 175 mL the lateral angle. Tell: blunting fills the angle in, while the deep sulcus sign is a darkened, deepened angle, the look of air.

Air in the mediastinal tissues is pneumomediastinum, found as subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and a crunch heard with each heartbeat. Tell: the dark area here lies at the costophrenic angle of the pleural space.
An infiltrate is fluid within the lung itself, as in pneumonia, distinct from fluid in the pleural space. Tell: a darkened, deepened angle means air in the pleural space, not fluid-filled lung.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has tense ascites and a new right pleural effusion. He has no orthopnea, leg edema or known heart disease, and no fever or cough. Pleural fluid protein is 1.2 g/dL with serum protein 5.8 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 70 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 180 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). Which is the most likely cause of the effusion?
opts: Tuberculosis is the leading cause of exudative effusion worldwide, with fever, night sweats, hemoptysis and weight loss. Tell: his fluid is a transudate with every criterion absent, and he has no infectious symptoms.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Protein ratio 1.2 / 5.8 = 0.21, lactate dehydrogenase ratio 70 / 180 = 0.39, and fluid lactate dehydrogenase 70 is under two-thirds of 280, about 187: all of Light's criteria are absent, a transudate. Cirrhosis with ascites sends peritoneal fluid across the diaphragm and lowers oncotic pressure.

Heart failure causes more than 90% of transudates, through increased capillary hydrostatic pressure. Tell: he has no orthopnea, leg edema or heart disease, and his ascites with cirrhosis explains the transudate.
ruled out by a stated finding
Pneumonia is the most common cause of exudative effusion, with fever, purulent sputum and pleuritic pain. Tell: he has no fever or cough, and his fluid meets none of Light's criteria.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 36-year-old woman with a hemothorax after a stab wound has a chest tube placed. Over the next 2 hours it drains blood at about 300 mL per hour, and her blood pressure is falling. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Chemical pleurodesis makes the pleural layers adhere to prevent recurrent pneumothorax or a recurring effusion. Tell: it does nothing to stop active bleeding into the chest.
Needle decompression relieves a tension pneumothorax when no chest tube is at hand. Tell: she already has a chest tube, and her problem is blood loss, not trapped air.

Correct. The chest tube evacuates and quantifies the bleeding, and blood loss over 200 mL per hour calls for thoracotomy, an open approach to the intrathoracic space. Persistent hemorrhage or shock is the indication for surgery, and she has both.

Continued drainage alone fits bleeding that slows below the surgical threshold. Tell: her output of about 300 mL per hour exceeds 200 mL per hour and her pressure is falling, so the tube has done its job of measuring and surgery follows.

set1.q: A 25-year-old woman has sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea at rest. Her upright chest radiograph is reviewed for a pneumothorax. Which radiographic finding establishes the diagnosis?
opts: Blunting of the costophrenic angle is the upright-film sign of pleural fluid, 75 mL posteriorly and 175 mL laterally. Tell: a pneumothorax is air, shown by the visceral pleural line, not by a fluid-filled angle.

A straight line with no meniscus marks a hemopneumothorax, where air sits above fluid in the pleural space. Tell: she has no reason for blood in the chest, and the diagnostic sign of pleural air alone is the visceral pleural line.

Bronchovascular markings are not typically visible beyond the visceral pleural edge, because only air lies there. Tell: markings past the line argue against a pneumothorax; their absence beyond a thin line supports it.

Correct. The diagnosis is established by demonstrating a visceral pleural line, the interface of lung and pleural air. It is a thin, sharp line convex outward toward the chest wall, with no bronchovascular markings visible beyond it.

set1.q: A 25-year-old man has a stab wound to the right chest wall. Air can be heard moving through the wound, which draws air into the pleural space with each inhalation, and breath sounds are diminished on the right. How is his pneumothorax classified?
opts: Spontaneous pneumothorax means no thoracic trauma; primary adds no underlying lung abnormality. Tell: he has a penetrating stab wound, which makes his pneumothorax traumatic.
ruled out by a stated finding
Iatrogenic pneumothorax is pleural injury from a medical intervention, such as thoracentesis or a subclavian vein catheter. Tell: his wound came from a stabbing, not a procedure.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. An open pneumothorax has a direct wound in the chest wall that allows air to enter the pleural space during inhalation, and it can lead to a sucking chest wound. A penetrating stab wound is a traumatic cause.

A closed pneumothorax has no external wound; air enters the pleural space from the lung because of broken ribs or internal injuries. Tell: his chest wall is open, and air enters through the wound itself.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 23-year-old man has a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax with an apex-to-cupola distance of 2 cm on his upright chest radiograph. He has mild pleuritic pain, no significant dyspnea and stable vital signs. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Correct. A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax, under 3 cm at the apex, with minimal symptoms is observed with adequate analgesia and oxygen at 100% by non-rebreather mask, which accelerates resorption of air. A repeat film confirms it has not expanded, and he is discharged if it is stable and he is asymptomatic.

A chest tube treats a moderate or large primary pneumothorax, over 3 cm at the apex, with moderate or severe symptoms, or a failed observation or aspiration. Tell: his is 2 cm with mild pain and no failed treatment.
Catheter aspiration treats a small primary pneumothorax when significant dyspnea persists after analgesia. Tell: he has mild pain without significant dyspnea, so observation fits first.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis is the treatment for a recurrent primary pneumothorax and the best preventive procedure. Tell: this is his first episode, small and minimally symptomatic.

set1.q: A 57-year-old man has 5 days of fever, cough with purulent sputum and right pleuritic chest pain, and a right pleural effusion is tapped. Pleural fluid protein is 4.4 g/dL with serum protein 7.2 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 240 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 210 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). Which is the most likely cause of the effusion?
opts: Nephrotic syndrome causes a transudate by lowering oncotic pressure as albumin is lost. Tell: his protein ratio of 0.61 and lactate dehydrogenase values mark an exudate, which fits his pneumonia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Protein ratio 4.4 / 7.2 = 0.61, above 0.5; lactate dehydrogenase ratio 240 / 210 = 1.14, above 0.6; fluid lactate dehydrogenase 240 exceeds two-thirds of 280, about 187. The fluid is an exudate, pneumonia is the most common cause of exudative effusion, and fever with purulent sputum and pleuritic pain is its clue set.

Heart failure causes more than 90% of transudates, with edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Tell: his fluid meets all three of Light's criteria, an exudate, and his story is an infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

Cirrhosis with ascites causes a transudate, through peritoneal fluid crossing the diaphragm and low oncotic pressure. Tell: his fluid is exudative by every criterion, and he has fever with purulent sputum.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 71-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease uses noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation at home every night. He is admitted with a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, and air is still bubbling through his chest tube, showing an active air leak. Which of his therapies should be held for now?
opts: Most secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are treated with chest tube insertion. Tell: the tube is draining his leak and stays; the positive pressure from his home ventilator is what pauses.

Correct. Positive-pressure therapies are held during an active air leak. His nightly noninvasive ventilation is positive pressure, and air still bubbling through his tube shows the leak is active, so it is paused until the leak has closed.

Oxygen accelerates resorption of pleural air and is part of observing a small pneumothorax. Tell: oxygen is not a positive-pressure therapy; the device to hold is the one that pushes air under pressure.
Adequate analgesia is part of pneumothorax care. Tell: pain control does nothing to an air leak; the therapy to hold during an active leak is positive pressure.

set1.q: A 78-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a second secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, now drained by a chest tube. His team judges that he cannot tolerate general anesthesia, so surgery is not an option. Which procedure best lowers his risk of another recurrence?
opts: Thoracoscopic surgery is indicated for secondary pneumothorax and recurrence, but its risks include those of general anesthesia. Tell: his team has ruled out anesthesia, so surgery is off the table.
ruled out by a stated finding
Underlying pulmonary disease and recurrent pneumothorax are both contraindications to catheter aspiration. Tell: he has both, and aspiration would not prevent recurrence anyway.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Most secondary spontaneous pneumothoraces are treated with a chest tube and may go on to thoracoscopic surgery or thoracotomy with bleb stapling and pleural abrasion. If surgery is not an option, chemical pleurodesis via the chest tube is used: a sclerosant such as talc makes the pleural layers adhere.

Mechanical pleurodesis is manual abrasion of the pleura performed through a surgical intervention. Tell: it needs the operation he cannot have; the chemical route goes through the tube he already has.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 63-year-old man on peritoneal dialysis develops a right pleural effusion. He has no heart failure, and his serum albumin is normal at 4.0 g/dL (normal 3.5-5.0 g/dL). He asks how the dialysis fluid in his abdomen could reach his chest. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Reduced intravascular oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia drives the effusions of nephrotic syndrome and cirrhosis. Tell: his albumin is normal at 4.0 g/dL, so oncotic pressure is not the problem.
ruled out by a stated finding

Decreased or blocked lymphatic drainage is the mechanism in malignancy and trauma. Tell: dialysis fluid reaches the chest by crossing the diaphragm through microperforations, not by blocking lymphatics.

Correct. In cirrhosis and peritoneal dialysis, increased peritoneal fluid leaks, or extravasates, across the diaphragm through microperforations into the pleural space. Peritoneal dialysis is listed among the conditions associated with transudates.
Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure is how heart failure causes effusion. Tell: he has no heart failure; his fluid comes from the peritoneal cavity itself.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 23-year-old tall, thin man has acute dyspnea and sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain that began at rest. His respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, heart rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and he speaks in whole sentences. Which is the initial test?
opts: Correct. The initial test for pneumothorax is a standard upright chest radiograph. The diagnosis is established by showing the visceral pleural line, a thin, sharp line convex toward the chest wall with no bronchovascular markings beyond it, and his stable vital signs leave time for the film.

Thoracic computed tomography is the best modality for the presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, the diagnostic gold standard, but it is not where the workup starts. Tell: gold standard and best initial test are different questions; the upright film comes first.

An arterial blood gas is often unnecessary; it is indicated for severe underlying lung disease or persistent distress with saturation under 92% despite treatment. Tell: he is healthy and saturating 96%, and a blood gas cannot show pleural air.
ruled out by a stated finding

A supine film is where pleural air collects laterally and shows as the deep sulcus sign, a picture used when the patient cannot sit up. Tell: he can sit up, and the standard initial test is the upright chest radiograph.

set1.q: A 21-year-old tall, thin man is recovering from his first primary spontaneous pneumothorax. He smokes a pack of cigarettes a day, and his father had the same condition. Before discharge, the clinician counsels him on the risk factor he can change. Which risk factor should the counseling address?
opts: Correct. Smoking is a significant risk factor for primary spontaneous pneumothorax and the one he can change. Recurrence approaches 50% within three years of a first episode, so education includes the importance of smoking cessation and help to quit if he is willing.
Family history is listed as a risk factor, an inherited association, but it cannot be changed. Tell: counseling targets what he can modify; his family history instead prompts a genetics referral.

Being a tall, thin young male is the classic profile for primary spontaneous pneumothorax, but body build is not something he can change. Tell: the modifiable, significant risk factor in his history is the pack a day.

Primary spontaneous pneumothorax often occurs at rest and may occur during strenuous exercise; exercise is not one of its listed risk factors. Tell: the risk factors are build, age 20-40, male sex, smoking and family history, and only smoking can change.

set1.q: A 27-year-old man with pneumomediastinum after forceful breath-holding while inhaling an illicit drug develops worsening dyspnea, subcutaneous emphysema spreading up his neck and a falling oxygen saturation despite oxygen. His airway is being supported. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Pneumomediastinum is usually managed conservatively, but if it is severe, cardiothoracic surgery is consulted emergently, after the airway is assessed and maintained. His worsening dyspnea, spreading emphysema and falling saturation despite oxygen mark severe disease.
An outpatient visit fits a stable patient whose air is expected to absorb with conservative care. Tell: his disease is worsening despite oxygen, which calls for an emergent consult.

Genetics referral is recommended after spontaneous pneumothorax when the family history shows the same condition. Tell: his problem is severe mediastinal air after drug inhalation, which needs surgery now.

Esophageal perforation is one cause of pneumomediastinum, and an identified cause is treated. Tell: his history points to a pressure rise from breath-holding, and his worsening state needs an emergent surgical consult, not a clinic visit.

set1.q: A 31-year-old man has had sharp, well-localized left chest pain for 3 days after a viral upper respiratory infection. The pain worsens with deep breathing and coughing, and a pleural friction rub (a scratching, creaking sound) disappears when he holds his breath. Myocardial infarction, pneumothorax and pneumonia have been excluded, and his chest radiograph is normal. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: A chest tube drains fluid or air from the pleural space in pneumothorax or pleural effusion. Tell: his chest radiograph is normal, so there is no air or fluid to drain; inflamed pleura is treated medically.

Pleurodesis instills a sclerosant so that the two pleural layers adhere, to prevent recurrent pneumothorax or a recurring effusion. Tell: obliterating the pleural space is a procedure for recurrent air or fluid, not for a first episode of pleural inflammation.

Oxygen at 100% by non-rebreather mask accelerates resorption of air in a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Tell: his film shows no pleural air to resorb; his pleuritic pain calls for anti-inflammatory treatment.

Correct. Pleurisy is treated by treating the underlying condition and giving nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. His viral infection is an infectious cause, the dangerous causes are excluded, and the anti-inflammatory drug addresses the parietal pleural inflammation behind his pain.

set1.q: A 33-year-old man with a tension pneumothorax after a gunshot wound has hypotension, tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins and absent left breath sounds. His family asks why his blood pressure has fallen. Which mechanism explains his hypotension?
opts: Bleeding into the pleural space is hemothorax, and trauma is its most common cause. Tell: his distended neck veins and tracheal shift fit trapped air impeding venous return, the tension mechanism.
Tension pneumothorax lowers cardiac output, it does not raise it. Tell: the mediastinal shift decreases venous return to the heart, so output and blood pressure both fall.

The listed consequences of tension pneumothorax are decreased venous return and cardiac output, with hypotension, tracheal deviation and neck vein distention. Tell: his pressure falls because filling falls, not because the heart slows.
Less venous return to the heart

Correct. In tension pneumothorax, air trapped by a one-way valve shifts the mediastinum to the contralateral side. Venous return to the heart decreases, cardiac output falls, and hypotension follows, along with tracheal deviation and neck vein distention.

set1.q: A 71-year-old woman has a new left pleural effusion with no clear clinical cause, and diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. Pleural fluid protein is 2.1 g/dL with serum protein 7.0 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 210 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 450 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). How is the effusion classified by Light's criteria?
opts: Correct. Protein ratio 2.1 / 7.0 = 0.30, not above 0.5. Lactate dehydrogenase ratio 210 / 450 = 0.47, not above 0.6. But fluid lactate dehydrogenase 210 exceeds two-thirds of the 280 upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase, about 187: met, so the fluid is an exudate.
The protein ratio is 2.1 / 7.0 = 0.30, below the 0.5 cutoff. Tell: her exudate criterion is the fluid lactate dehydrogenase of 210, above two-thirds of the 280 upper limit, about 187.

The ratio is 210 / 450 = 0.47, under 0.6, because her serum lactate dehydrogenase is itself high. Tell: the third criterion compares the fluid value with the normal upper limit, and 210 is above two-thirds of 280, about 187.
A transudate needs all three criteria absent. Tell: both ratios miss, but her fluid lactate dehydrogenase of 210 is above two-thirds of the 280 upper limit, about 187, so one criterion is met.

set1.q: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and a 40-pack-year smoking history has sudden sharp left chest pain that worsens with deep breathing. Before the pain is attributed to pleurisy, which condition belongs among those that must be considered immediately?
opts: Correct. Pleuritic pain demands immediate consideration of the dangerous causes: myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism. Only after those are weighed are the other causes, such as rib fracture, costochondritis, vertebral fracture or zoster nerve pain, considered.

Costochondritis, inflammation of the costal cartilage, belongs to the second group, the other causes to consider. Tell: it is not one of the dangerous conditions weighed first, which are myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism.

Rib fracture is listed with the other causes of chest pain, after the dangerous ones. Tell: the conditions that must be considered immediately are the dangerous ones, and aortic dissection is on that list.

Nerve root pain from herpes zoster is another of the other causes to consider once the dangerous ones are excluded. Tell: the immediate list is myocardial infarction, pericarditis, aortic dissection, pneumonia, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man has a bloody-appearing pleural effusion after a fall. The pleural fluid hematocrit is 30%, and his blood hematocrit is 40% (normal 41-53%). How is the effusion classified?
opts: Empyema is purulent fluid in the pleural space, usually after bacterial pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion. Tell: his fluid is bloody after a fall, not purulent after an infection.

Correct. A pleural fluid hematocrit over 50% of the peripheral blood hematocrit defines a hemothorax, while under 50% marks a hemorrhagic effusion. His fluid hematocrit of 30% is 75% of his blood value of 40%, well over half, and trauma causes most hemothoraces.
A hemorrhagic effusion is bloody fluid whose hematocrit is under 50% of the blood hematocrit. Tell: 30 divided by 40 is 75%, above the 50% cutoff, so this is a hemothorax.
Chylothorax is lipid from chyle in the pleural space, with milky fluid and elevated triglycerides. Tell: his fluid is bloody, and its hematocrit is the deciding measurement.

set1.q: A 30-year-old man has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. His respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, heart rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and he speaks in whole sentences. How is he classified by the American College of Chest Physicians stability definition?
opts: The respiratory-rate criterion is under 24 breaths per minute. Tell: his rate of 18 meets it easily; his failed criterion is the heart rate of 128, over the upper bound of 120 beats per minute.
ruled out by a stated finding
The saturation criterion is a room-air oxygen saturation over 90%. Tell: his 97% on room air passes; the fast heart rate of 128 is what fails the definition.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The heart-rate criterion has two bounds: over 60 and under 120 beats per minute. His rate of 128 is above 120, so he fails it even though his respiratory rate of 18, normal pressure, saturation of 97% and full sentences pass; anyone who misses a criterion is unstable.
Stability needs every criterion, including a heart rate under 120. Tell: his rate of 128 is above that upper bound, so he cannot be classed as stable despite his other values.

set1.q: A 22-year-old man with Marfan syndrome, who is tall and thin, develops sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea while playing video games. He has never smoked. His upright chest radiograph shows a visceral pleural line on the left. How is his pneumothorax classified?
opts: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is classically seen in tall, thin young males aged 20-40 with no underlying lung abnormality. Tell: his Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disease that moves the episode into the secondary group.

Traumatic pneumothorax needs a history of blunt or penetrating thoracic trauma, such as a stab wound or a rib fracture that tears the lung. Tell: his pain began while he sat playing video games, with no injury.
ruled out by a stated finding
Iatrogenic pneumothorax follows a medical intervention such as thoracentesis, subclavian vein catheter placement, bronchoscopy or mechanical ventilation. Tell: no procedure preceded his symptoms.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Spontaneous means no thoracic trauma, and secondary means an underlying abnormality. Connective tissue disease such as Marfan syndrome is listed among the risk factors for secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, so his tall, thin build does not make this primary.

set1.q: A 61-year-old woman being treated with antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia still has fever and pleuritic pain after several days, and her parapneumonic effusion has grown. Thoracentesis returns thick purulent fluid. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Antibiotics are half of empyema treatment, but pus in the pleural space also has to be drained. Tell: her pneumonia did not resolve on antibiotics, and the treatment pairs drainage with antibiotics.

Chemical pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space, mainly for recurrent malignant effusions or recurrent pneumothorax. Tell: an infected pleural space needs drainage and antibiotics, not obliteration.
Diuretics are the initial treatment for transudates secondary to heart failure. Tell: her fluid is pus from an infection, an exudative process that diuretics do not address.

Correct. Empyema is purulent fluid in the pleural space, and bacterial pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion is its most common precursor. It is suspected when pneumonia does not resolve with therapy and diagnosed by purulent material on thoracentesis; treatment is drainage and antibiotics, treating the underlying disease and analgesia, and prompt therapy is critical.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man has a new moderate left pleural effusion on chest radiograph. He has no heart, liver or kidney disease, no fever or cough, and no history of cancer or trauma, so no clinical cause is apparent. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Diuretics are the initial treatment for transudates secondary to heart failure. Tell: he has no heart disease and no known cause, so the fluid is sampled before any treatment is chosen.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed when there is a new pleural effusion with no clinical cause. It removes 50-100 mL for visualization and analysis, sent for protein, lactate dehydrogenase, cell count, Gram stain, cytology and culture, and ultrasound is used to guide it.

Chemical pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space, often for recurrent malignant effusions in an expandable lung. Tell: his effusion is new and has no diagnosis yet, so the fluid must be analyzed first.
An indwelling tunneled pleural catheter is drained at home for rapidly recurring fluid or a short prognosis, as palliative care. Tell: he has a first, undiagnosed effusion, not a recurring one.

set1.q: A 24-year-old woman with an inherited bleeding disorder has a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax with an apex-to-cupola distance of 2 cm. She still has significant dyspnea after adequate analgesia, a situation in which catheter aspiration is usually offered. Which feature of her history contraindicates catheter aspiration?
opts: Small means under 3 cm at the apex, and a small primary pneumothorax with significant dyspnea after analgesia is the presentation that catheter aspiration treats. Tell: her 2 cm size points toward aspiration, not away from it.

Significant dyspnea after analgesia is the indication for catheter aspiration in a small primary pneumothorax. Tell: the dyspnea is why aspiration was considered; her bleeding disorder is the listed contraindication.

Correct. A small primary spontaneous pneumothorax, under 3 cm at the apex, with significant dyspnea after analgesia is treated with catheter aspiration. Bleeding disorders are on the list of contraindications to aspiration, so her inherited bleeding disorder removes the option.

A recurrent pneumothorax contraindicates catheter aspiration; a first episode does not. Tell: her first episode is exactly where aspiration usually fits, and the bleeding disorder is what rules it out.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man develops a right pleural effusion 5 days after thoracic surgery. Thoracentesis returns milky white fluid. Which pleural fluid result confirms the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Purulent material on thoracentesis diagnoses empyema, usually after bacterial pneumonia. Tell: his fluid is milky after thoracic surgery, the picture of chyle, and fluid appearance alone is not diagnostic without the triglyceride level.
Cytology detects malignant cells in a malignant effusion. Tell: his effusion followed thoracic surgery with milky fluid, which points to thoracic duct injury and a triglyceride-rich fluid.
A pleural fluid hematocrit over 50% of the blood hematocrit defines a hemothorax, with bloody fluid. Tell: his fluid is milky, not bloody, so the confirming test is the triglyceride level.

Correct. Chylothorax is thoracic duct disruption that lets lipid from chyle collect in the pleural space, and trauma such as thoracic surgery is its most common cause. Thoracentesis shows milky fluid with elevated triglycerides.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman who was treated for breast cancer 8 years ago has a new right pleural effusion with no other clinical cause, and diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. Which pleural fluid study is sent specifically to detect a malignant effusion?
opts: Correct. Pleural fluid is sent for protein, lactate dehydrogenase, white cell count with differential, Gram stain, cytology and microbiological culture, and cytology is the study that detects malignant effusions. Malignant effusions can occur years after a cancer diagnosis, and breast carcinoma is among their leading causes.
A Gram stain looks for bacteria, the concern in a parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Tell: her history points to cancer returning, and malignant cells are found by cytology.
Culture grows organisms from an infected effusion such as empyema. Tell: she has no fever or pneumonia, and culture does not detect malignant cells; cytology does.
Elevated triglycerides in milky fluid identify a chylothorax from thoracic duct disruption. Tell: her concern is malignancy years after breast cancer, which cytology addresses.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops a spontaneous pneumothorax. His daughter, who had a pneumothorax at age 24 with no lung disease, asks how his episode is likely to differ from hers. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Observation followed by discharge fits a small primary pneumothorax that stays stable on repeat film. Tell: a secondary pneumothorax is more life-threatening because of lost pulmonary reserve and calls for hospitalization for monitoring.

Correct. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is the most common cause of secondary spontaneous pneumothorax. The symptoms are those of a primary episode but generally greater, because the underlying disease leaves less pulmonary reserve; the event can be life-threatening and needs more immediate intervention.

Good pulmonary reserve, with severe respiratory distress uncommon, describes primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a young adult without lung disease, as his daughter had. Tell: his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease removes that reserve and makes the event more dangerous.

The physical examination is the same as in a primary episode, but the symptoms are generally greater and care is more urgent. Tell: a secondary pneumothorax, even a small one, is managed with hospitalization, unlike a stable small primary one.

set2.q: A 27-year-old man has a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax. On his upright chest radiograph, the apex-to-cupola distance is 4 cm and the interpleural distance at the level of the hilum is 1.5 cm. How is its size classified by the American College of Chest Physicians definition?
opts: Correct. The American College of Chest Physicians sizes a pneumothorax by the apex-to-cupola distance: under 3 cm is small, 3 cm or more is large. His 4 cm apex-to-cupola distance makes it large; the interpleural distance at the hilum is the British guideline measurement.
The interpleural distance at the level of the hilum is the British guideline measurement, not the American one. Tell: the American definition reads the apex-to-cupola distance, which is 4 cm here.
The apex-to-cupola distance is the right landmark, but small means under 3 cm. Tell: his apex-to-cupola distance is 4 cm, past the 3 cm cutoff, so the pneumothorax is large.
The hilum distance is the British landmark, not the one the American definition reads. Tell: the American College of Chest Physicians label of large comes from the 4 cm apex-to-cupola distance.

set2.q: A 27-year-old woman is being discharged after her primary spontaneous pneumothorax has resolved. She has a flight booked for a conference and asks for advice about air travel. Which advice is accurate?
opts: Delay flying; confirm with a film

Correct. Air travel is delayed for 7-14 days after resolution, and resolution is confirmed with a chest X-ray before she flies. Follow-up films verify complete lung re-expansion, and she is also counseled on recurrence and, if she smokes, on stopping.
Fly once the chest pain is gone
Pain relief does not show that the lung has fully re-expanded. Tell: the advice is a delay after resolution, with resolution confirmed on a chest X-ray, not judged by symptoms.
Fly if her oxygen level is normal
A normal oxygen saturation does not confirm that the pneumothorax has resolved. Tell: the check before flying is a chest X-ray showing re-expansion, after a waiting period.
Air travel is delayed, not forbidden for life. Tell: the guide is to wait after resolution and confirm it with a film; avoiding scuba diving is the lasting restriction.

set2.q: A 35-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash with decreased breath sounds on the right. His respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute, heart rate 126 beats per minute and blood pressure 90/58 mm Hg, his trachea is midline and his neck veins are flat. The team needs a rapid answer at the bedside about a pneumothorax. Which test best fits?
opts: A lateral decubitus film, taken with the patient lying on the side of the effusion, shows small amounts of pleural fluid. Tell: it is a fluid study for a stable patient, not a rapid bedside pneumothorax test in an unstable one.

Correct. Lung ultrasound is becoming an indispensable bedside tool for the rapid diagnosis of pneumothorax and is beneficial for the unstable patient; absent lung sliding marks a pneumothorax. His tachycardia and hypotension make him unstable, so the test has to come to him.

Computed tomography is the best modality for the presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, but it is impractical in a time-critical situation. Tell: an unstable trauma patient needs a bedside answer, not a trip to the scanner.
ruled out by a stated finding

An arterial blood gas is often unnecessary and depends on ventilation status and compensation; it usually shows hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis. Tell: a blood gas cannot show where the air is, and the bedside image can.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a chylothorax after thoracic surgery, managed with a chest tube. Over several days the tube has drained large volumes of milky fluid, and she is losing weight. Which practice should be avoided?
opts: Decreasing long-chain triglycerides in the diet decreases chyle drainage, because they are absorbed through the lymphatic system. Tell: this nutrition step lowers her chyle output and is recommended.
Intermittent thoracentesis is one of the two drainage approaches for chylothorax, beside a chest tube. Tell: the method is acceptable; it is the excessive volume removed that harms her nutrition.

Correct. Chylothorax is managed with chest tube placement or intermittent thoracentesis while avoiding excessive drainage, because excessive loss of chyle can impact nutritional status. Her large volumes and weight loss show that risk.
Octreotide is used in chylothorax to decrease chyle drainage. Tell: it lowers the very output she is losing, so it is a treatment to use, not one to avoid.

set2.q: A 26-year-old woman has a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Her respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and she speaks in whole sentences. How is she classified by the American College of Chest Physicians stability definition?
opts: The respiratory-rate criterion is under 24 breaths per minute. Tell: her rate of 20 meets it, and her heart rate, pressure, saturation and speech pass too, so nothing makes her unstable.
ruled out by a stated finding

The heart-rate criterion is over 60 and under 120 beats per minute. Tell: her heart rate of 96 sits inside that range, so tachycardia has not crossed the cutoff of 120, and her other values pass as well.
ruled out by a stated finding
The saturation criterion is a room-air oxygen saturation over 90%. Tell: her 96% on room air clears it, and her respiratory rate, heart rate, pressure and whole sentences meet the other criteria.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Every criterion is met: respiratory rate 20, under 24; heart rate 96, between 60 and 120; normal blood pressure; room-air saturation 96%, over 90%; and whole sentences. Stability requires all of these, and she has all of them.

set2.q: A 23-year-old woman has sudden fever and paroxysms of knife-like pleuritic pain lasting 15-30 minutes after a gastrointestinal illness, with tender intercostal muscles and a normal chest radiograph. Which laboratory finding supports the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Purulent fluid on thoracentesis diagnoses empyema after bacterial pneumonia. Tell: her chest radiograph is normal, so there is no effusion to sample, and her disease sits in the intercostal muscles.
ruled out by a stated finding
Bloody pleural fluid suggests a hemothorax or malignancy. Tell: her film shows no effusion, and her tender muscles after a viral illness point to a muscle enzyme in the blood.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. In pleurodynia, the virus, often coxsackie B, targets the striated intercostal muscles, causing inflammation or necrosis that frequently raises serum creatine kinase. Elevated creatine kinase is its listed diagnostic finding, and the chest radiograph is usually normal.
Elevated triglycerides in milky pleural fluid identify a chylothorax. Tell: she has no effusion on a normal film; her disease is in the intercostal muscles, measured by serum creatine kinase.

set2.q: A 46-year-old woman falls from a ladder and fractures several left ribs. The skin over her chest is intact, and a chest radiograph shows a visceral pleural line on the left. How is her pneumothorax classified?
opts: An open traumatic pneumothorax has a direct chest wall wound that lets air in during inhalation. Tell: her skin is intact, so the air came from the torn lung, not through the chest wall.
ruled out by a stated finding

Iatrogenic pneumothorax follows a medical intervention such as bronchoscopy or mechanical ventilation. Tell: her pneumothorax followed a fall with rib fractures, which is thoracic trauma, not a procedure.
ruled out by a stated finding
Spontaneous pneumothorax means no thoracic trauma, and primary means no underlying lung abnormality. Tell: she fell and broke ribs, which is thoracic trauma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Blunt chest trauma in which a rib fracture tears the lung is a traumatic pneumothorax. With no external wound, air enters the pleural space from the lung because of the broken ribs, which makes it closed.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: A 38-year-old man has a new right pleural effusion. For 2 months he has had fevers, drenching night sweats, hemoptysis and a 6 kg weight loss. He has no leg swelling or orthopnea and no purulent sputum. Which is the most likely cause of his effusion?
opts: Hemoptysis on its own raises the question of malignancy. Tell: his full set of fever, night sweats, hemoptysis and weight loss is the tuberculosis clue set, and the fevers and sweats are not part of the malignancy clue.

Heart failure is suggested by lower extremity edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and it is the leading cause of effusion overall. Tell: he has none of those, and fevers with night sweats point to an infection.
ruled out by a stated finding
Pneumonia is suggested by fever, purulent sputum and pleuritic chest pain. Tell: he has no purulent sputum, and two months of night sweats and weight loss fit tuberculosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Fever, night sweats, hemoptysis and weight loss together are the extrapulmonary clue set that points to tuberculosis in a patient with an effusion. Tuberculosis is also the leading cause of exudative effusion worldwide.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man has sharp chest pain that worsens with deep breaths. On auscultation there is a grating, creaking friction rub over the lower anterior chest, and the clinician is unsure whether it arises from the pleura or the pericardium. Which bedside maneuver best separates the two?
opts: Correct. A pleural friction rub disappears when the patient holds his breath, and that is the feature that differentiates it from a pericardial friction rub. The pleural rub comes from inflamed pleural layers rubbing together during respiration, so stopping respiration stops the sound.

Dullness to percussion is the sign of fluid collecting over a pleural effusion. Tell: percussion answers whether fluid is present under the chest wall; it does not tell a pleural rub from a pericardial one, and breath holding does.

Tactile fremitus is decreased when pleural air or fluid impedes the vibrations reaching the chest wall, as in pneumothorax or effusion. Tell: fremitus speaks to air or fluid in the pleural space, not to the source of a rub; breath holding settles that.

Coughing exacerbates pleuritic pain, along with deep breathing, movement and sneezing, so it helps describe the pain. Tell: the rub's source is decided by stopping respiration, and a pleural rub disappears when he holds his breath.

set2.q: A 29-year-old woman with pleurisy has sharp pain at the base of the right chest and also pain at the tip of her right shoulder, although her shoulder examination is normal. She asks why her shoulder hurts. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Muscle strain is on the differential for chest pain, but her shoulder examination is normal and the shoulder pain accompanies pleurisy at the right base. Tell: same-side shoulder pain with diaphragmatic pleurisy is referred through phrenic nerve fibers.

Correct. The parietal pleura has sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerve fibers. When the inflamed parietal pleura lies on the central diaphragm, which is innervated by phrenic fibers, pain may be felt in the shoulder or neck on the same side, as hers is.

Intercostal fibers supply the parietal pleura lining the chest wall, which is why pleurisy produces well-localized sharp pain over the chest wall. Tell: pain referred to the same-side shoulder comes from the central diaphragm and its phrenic fibers.

The visceral pleura covers the lungs and has no sensory innervation, so it cannot generate her pain at all. Tell: pleuritic pain arises from the parietal pleura, and the shoulder component from its phrenic-innervated diaphragmatic part.

set2.q: A 41-year-old woman on a ventilator after a fall suddenly becomes hypotensive at 74/46 mm Hg. Her trachea has shifted to the right, her neck veins are distended and breath sounds are absent on the left. No chest tube kit is readily available on the unit. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Computed tomography is the best test for the presence, size and location of a pneumothorax, but it is impractical in a time-critical situation. Tell: she is hypotensive with tension signs, and every minute counts.

Correct. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and time is critical. Immediate chest tube placement is ideal, but when a chest tube is not readily available, immediate needle decompression is performed, followed by a moderate or large chest tube and admission.

Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency diagnosed clinically: there is no time for the X-ray. Tell: hypotension, tracheal shift, distended neck veins and absent breath sounds are enough to act on.
Tension pneumothorax and hemodynamic instability are both contraindications to catheter aspiration. Tell: she has both; the emergency tool without a chest tube is needle decompression.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 26-year-old tall, thin man has acute dyspnea and sharp left-sided chest pain that worsens with deep breathing. His upright chest radiograph shows a thin, sharp visceral pleural line on the left with no lung markings beyond it. Which examination finding is expected on the left?
opts: Tactile fremitus is decreased or absent over a pneumothorax, because pleural air impedes the transmission of vibrations from the larynx to the chest surface. Tell: air in the pleural space lowers fremitus, as fluid does in an effusion; neither raises it.

Bronchial breath sounds increase toward the top of a pleural effusion, above the fluid. Tell: over a pneumothorax, breath sounds are diminished or absent on the affected side because pleural air transmits sound poorly.

Correct. Percussion over a primary spontaneous pneumothorax is hyperresonant, because air fills the pleural space between the lung and the chest wall. His film confirms that air: a visceral pleural line with no bronchovascular markings beyond it.
Dullness over fluid is the percussion sign of a pleural effusion. Tell: his film shows pleural air outlined by a visceral pleural line, not fluid, and air percusses hyperresonant.

set2.q: A 62-year-old woman with a new pleural effusion undergoes diagnostic thoracentesis. Pleural fluid protein is 3.9 g/dL with serum protein 6.5 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 150 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 200 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). How many of Light's criteria does the fluid meet, and what does that make it?
opts: A transudate needs every criterion absent. Tell: her protein ratio, 3.9 / 6.5 = 0.60, and her lactate dehydrogenase ratio, 150 / 200 = 0.75, both cross their cutoffs.

Exudate is right, but the count misses a criterion. Tell: both ratios are met, protein 0.60 above 0.5 and lactate dehydrogenase 0.75 above 0.6; only the level criterion, 150 against about 187, is not.

Correct. Protein ratio 3.9 / 6.5 = 0.60, above 0.5: met. Lactate dehydrogenase ratio 150 / 200 = 0.75, above 0.6: met. Fluid lactate dehydrogenase 150 is under two-thirds of the 280 upper limit, about 187: not met. Two of three, and one is already enough for an exudate.
Exudate is right, but the third criterion is not met. Tell: fluid lactate dehydrogenase of 150 is under two-thirds of the 280 upper limit of normal serum lactate dehydrogenase, about 187.

set2.q: A 24-year-old tall, thin man has sudden dyspnea and sharp right-sided chest pain that began while he was sitting at his desk. He smokes cigarettes. He is tachypneic and tachycardic, with decreased chest excursion on the right, decreased tactile fremitus (vibrations from the larynx poorly transmitted to the chest wall) on the right, hyperresonance to percussion on the right and diminished breath sounds on the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pleurisy brings sharp pain worse with breathing and a pleural friction rub, with palpation and percussion depending on the underlying condition. Tell: hyperresonance with decreased fremitus and diminished breath sounds means air in the pleural space, not inflammation alone.

Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinal tissues, found as palpable subcutaneous emphysema in the neck and a crunch heard with each heartbeat. Tell: his findings sit in one hemithorax, with hyperresonance and quiet breath sounds on that side.

Correct. A tall, thin young man who smokes fits primary spontaneous pneumothorax, which often occurs at rest with acute dyspnea and ipsilateral pleuritic pain. Decreased excursion and fremitus, hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds on one side follow because pleural air blocks the transmission of vibration and sound.

An effusion also decreases fremitus and breath sounds, because fluid obstructs the transmission of vibrations. Tell: fluid is dull to percussion, and his right chest is hyperresonant, the percussion note of air.

set2.q: A 77-year-old man has a new right pleural effusion with no clear clinical cause, and diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. Pleural fluid protein is 1.8 g/dL with serum protein 6.9 g/dL (normal 6.0-8.3 g/dL). Pleural fluid lactate dehydrogenase is 80 units/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 190 units/L (normal 140-280 units/L). How is the effusion classified by Light's criteria?
opts: The level criterion needs fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two-thirds of the 280 upper limit, about 187. Tell: his fluid value is 80, well below it, so no criterion is met.

Correct. Protein ratio 1.8 / 6.9 = 0.26, not above 0.5. Lactate dehydrogenase ratio 80 / 190 = 0.42, not above 0.6. Fluid lactate dehydrogenase 80 is under two-thirds of the 280 upper limit, about 187. With all of Light's criteria absent, the fluid is a low-protein transudate.
The protein criterion needs a pleural to serum protein ratio above 0.5. Tell: his is 1.8 / 6.9 = 0.26, about half the cutoff, consistent with a low-protein transudate.
The ratio criterion needs pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase above 0.6. Tell: 80 / 190 = 0.42 falls short, and neither of the other two criteria is met.

set2.q: A 24-year-old man has a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. His respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute, heart rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and he speaks in whole sentences. How is he classified by the American College of Chest Physicians stability definition?
opts: The saturation criterion is a room-air oxygen saturation over 90%. Tell: his 95% on room air passes; it is his respiratory rate of 28, against a cutoff of under 24, that makes him unstable.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Stability requires all of: respiratory rate under 24 breaths per minute, heart rate over 60 and under 120, normal blood pressure, room-air saturation over 90% and whole sentences. His heart rate of 104, normal pressure, saturation of 95% and full sentences pass, but a rate of 28 fails, and every other patient is unstable.

Stability needs every criterion met, and one failure makes the patient unstable. Tell: his respiratory rate of 28 breaths per minute is above the cutoff of under 24, so he cannot be called stable despite his other normal values.
The heart-rate criterion is over 60 and under 120 beats per minute. Tell: his heart rate of 104 sits inside that range; the failed criterion is his respiratory rate of 28.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: An 18-year-old woman with spontaneous pneumomediastinum after an episode of violent coughing asks how coughing could put air in her chest. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: The listed causes of pneumomediastinum are alveolar rupture from high pressure, esophageal perforation, and esophageal or bowel rupture with air dissecting into the mediastinum. Tell: coughing raised the pressure that ruptured alveoli; no infection made gas.

Correct. Violent coughing is a sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure. Excessive intra-alveolar pressure leads to rupture of alveoli bordering the mediastinum, and the escaping air collects in the mediastinal tissues.
A chest wall wound let air in
A direct chest wall wound that lets air in during inhalation is an open pneumothorax. Tell: she has no wound; her air came from inside the lung after a pressure rise.

Rupture of an apical bleb, a small air space within the visceral pleura, causes spontaneous pneumothorax, with air in the pleural space. Tell: her air is in the mediastinum, from alveoli that border it.

set2.q: A 27-year-old man has simultaneous bilateral spontaneous pneumothoraces on his upright chest radiograph. He is stable while both sides are drained. Which definitive procedure is indicated?
opts: Correct. Bilateral pneumothorax is an indication for video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, an endoscopic procedure through small incisions that allows bleb stapling and pleurodesis. Catheter aspiration is contraindicated with bilateral pneumothoraces, and thoracoscopic surgery has supplanted open thoracotomy for pneumothorax.

Thoracoscopic surgery has supplanted thoracotomy as surgical treatment of pneumothorax; thoracotomy remains for complicated cases, at the price of more discomfort and cost. Tell: nothing in his case is complicated beyond the bilateral disease the thoracoscope handles.

Bilateral pneumothoraces are on the list of contraindications to catheter aspiration, with recurrence, trauma, tension and bleeding disorders. Tell: his bilateral disease rules aspiration out and is itself an indication for thoracoscopic surgery.
ruled out by a stated finding
Observation with 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask fits a small primary pneumothorax with minimal symptoms. Tell: bilateral pneumothoraces are a surgical indication, not a case for observation.

set2.q: A 47-year-old man had a traumatic hemothorax that was only partly drained, and a collection of blood remains in his pleural space weeks later. Which complication does this retained blood most directly risk?
opts: Chylothorax follows thoracic duct disruption, most often from trauma such as thoracic surgery, and fills the space with chyle. Tell: retained blood does not become chyle; it becomes a nidus for infection.
Pneumomediastinum is air in the mediastinal tissues after alveolar rupture or esophageal perforation. Tell: blood left in the pleural space risks infection, not mediastinal air.

Correct. Undrained blood collections serve as a primary nidus for infection, and a retained hemothorax leads directly to empyema, as well as fibrothorax and trapped lung. That is why tube thoracostomy, the essential first step, aims to evacuate the blood.
Tension pneumothorax is trapped air under a one-way valve with hypotension and tracheal deviation. Tell: retained blood is fluid, and its risk is infection of that fluid.

Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman is scheduled for pleurodesis after her third spontaneous pneumothorax. She asks what the procedure will do inside her chest. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Correct. Pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space by inducing inflammation there: an irritant causes adhesions of the two layers of pleura, which helps keep the lung inflated after pneumothorax and leaves no room for fluid in an effusion. It is used to prevent recurrent or treat resistant pneumothorax.

Stapling or resection of blebs is a separate step performed during video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery. Tell: pleurodesis bonds the parietal and visceral layers together; it does not close the blebs themselves.

A Heimlich valve is a one-way flutter valve that lets air escape through a chest tube. Tell: draining air empties the space for now, whereas pleurodesis obliterates the space so the lung cannot collapse away again.

Mechanical pleurodesis abrades the pleura and chemical pleurodesis instills a sclerosant such as talc; neither removes a layer. Tell: the goal is irritation that makes the two layers adhere, not taking either one away.

set2.q: A 29-year-old commercial airline pilot has recovered from his first primary spontaneous pneumothorax, and a follow-up film confirms that the lung has re-expanded. He does not smoke and has no family history of pneumothorax. Which referral is recommended?
opts: Correct. Pilots and divers need early surgical options for safety, and video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery closes leaks to prevent future collapses. Recurrence approaches 50% within three years, a risk his occupation cannot carry.
Genetics referral is recommended when the family history reveals spontaneous pneumothorax. Tell: he has no such family history; his occupation is what drives the referral.
ruled out by a stated finding
Smoking cessation is part of education after a spontaneous pneumothorax, because smoking raises recurrence risk. Tell: he does not smoke, so the program would not address his risk.
ruled out by a stated finding
Returning to the cockpit without a plan ignores a recurrence risk that approaches 50% within three years. Tell: pilots and divers are singled out for early surgical evaluation.

set2.q: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 2 days of sharp, well-localized pain over the left chest wall that worsens with deep breathing, coughing and sneezing. She is tachypneic, with limited chest wall expansion on the left. A pleural friction rub (a grating, creaking sound) is heard in both phases of respiration and disappears when she holds her breath. Her chest radiograph is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Costochondritis, inflammation of the costal cartilage, is among the other causes of chest pain to consider after the dangerous ones. Tell: her friction rub comes from inflamed pleural layers rubbing together with each breath, a pleural sign that cartilage inflammation does not explain.

A pneumothorax also brings acute pleuritic pain, but its examination is hyperresonance with diminished breath sounds, and its film shows a visceral pleural line. Tell: her chest radiograph is normal and she has a friction rub, not the quiet, hyperresonant chest of pleural air.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Pleurisy is inflammation of the parietal pleura, and inflammatory disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus are among its causes. Well-localized sharp pain made worse by breathing, coughing and sneezing, limited expansion on the affected side and a pleural friction rub fit, and a rub that disappears with breath holding comes from the pleura.

Pericarditis is one of the dangerous causes to consider first, and breath holding is the test that separates a pericardial friction rub from a pleural one. Tell: her rub disappeared when she held her breath, which marks it as pleural, not pericardial.

set2.q: A 52-year-old woman with a rib fracture from a fall becomes acutely hypotensive, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins and absent breath sounds on the left. A chest tube kit is at the bedside. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Admission follows decompression and chest tube insertion for tension pneumothorax. Tell: it is part of her care, while delaying treatment for a film is the error.
Chest tube at the midaxillary line
The typical chest tube site is the 4th or 5th intercostal space at the midaxillary line. Tell: placing her tube there is standard practice, not something to avoid.

Correct. Tension pneumothorax is a medical emergency and a clinical diagnosis: time is critical, and there is no time for the X-ray. With a chest tube readily available, immediate chest tube placement is ideal, so waiting for imaging only wastes the time she does not have.

Immediate chest tube placement is the ideal treatment for tension pneumothorax when a tube is readily available. Tell: her kit is at the bedside, so placing it now is the right move, not one to avoid.

set2.q: A 78-year-old woman with known heart failure has increasing lower extremity edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and her chest radiograph shows bilateral pleural effusions. She is comfortable at rest. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed for a new pleural effusion with no clinical cause. Tell: her heart failure story explains the bilateral effusions, so treating the cause comes first.
ruled out by a stated finding
Pleurodesis obliterates the pleural space and is often used for recurrent malignant effusions as palliative care. Tell: her effusions come from heart failure, treated by treating the heart failure.

An indwelling tunneled pleural catheter suits a non-expandable lung, rapidly recurring fluid or a short prognosis. Tell: she is comfortable, and her effusions should respond to treating the heart failure.

Correct. Her edema, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea give the effusions a clear clinical cause: heart failure, which raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes more than 90% of transudates. Effusions are managed by treating the underlying disorder, and diuretics are the initial treatment for heart failure transudates.

set2.q: A 31-year-old man undergoes catheter aspiration of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax through the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line. More than 2 liters of air have been withdrawn through the stopcock, and air is still coming back. What should the clinician suspect?
opts: Tension pneumothorax traps air under a one-way valve and shows hypotension, tracheal deviation and neck vein distention. Tell: he has no such signs; air that keeps returning past 2 liters points to an ongoing leak.
When the lung has re-expanded, there is no more pleural air to withdraw. Tell: air still coming back after more than 2 liters is the opposite signal, a leak that keeps refilling the space.
A hemothorax is blood in the pleural space, most often from trauma, and is drained with a chest tube. Tell: what keeps returning through his stopcock is air, which points to a leak, not bleeding.

Correct. During catheter aspiration, removal of more than 2 liters should raise concern for a persistent air leak: air keeps entering the pleural space as it is withdrawn. A post-procedure chest radiograph follows, and failure of aspiration is an indication for a chest tube.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman in the intensive care unit becomes acutely short of breath after an attempted subclavian vein catheter placement, and bedside lung ultrasound is performed over the left chest. Which ultrasound finding indicates a pneumothorax?
opts: Lung sliding present is the normal finding, the visceral pleura moving against the parietal pleura with breathing. Tell: a pneumothorax separates the layers, so sliding is absent.

The presence of B-lines is described as ruling out pneumothorax. Tell: B-lines argue against air in the pleural space, while absent lung sliding, with the stratosphere sign on M-mode, is the finding that indicates it.
The seashore pattern is the normal M-mode appearance. Tell: with a pneumothorax it is replaced by the stratosphere sign, parallel horizontal lines, and lung sliding is absent.

Correct. On lung ultrasound, lung sliding is present in the normal lung and absent with a pneumothorax, the primary finding that the pleural layers are no longer moving against each other. On M-mode, the stratosphere sign, parallel horizontal lines, replaces the normal seashore pattern.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following: 2. Pneumothorax 3. Spontaneous 4. Traumatic 5. Hemothorax 6. Chylothorax 7. Pleural effusion 8. Pneumomediastinum 9. Pleurodynia 10. Pleurisy 11. Empyema
set2.q: A 67-year-old man has progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Over the lower right chest there is dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus (vibrations from the larynx poorly felt on the chest wall) and diminished breath sounds, with bronchial breath sounds at the upper edge of the dull area. Which condition best explains these findings?
opts: Correct. Dyspnea and dry cough are the most common symptoms of pleural effusion. Fluid is dull to percussion and obstructs the transmission of vibrations, so fremitus decreases; breath sounds are diminished over the effusion, while bronchial breath sounds increase toward its top, exactly his examination.
Pneumothorax also decreases fremitus and breath sounds, because pleural air blocks transmission. Tell: air is hyperresonant to percussion, and his lower right chest is dull, the note of fluid.
ruled out by a stated finding

An infiltrate is fluid within the lung itself, while an effusion collects in the pleural space and pushes against the lung. Tell: dullness with quiet breath sounds over the area and bronchial sounds only at its upper edge is the effusion pattern.

Pleurisy is inflammation of the parietal pleura with sharp pain and a friction rub, and its palpation and percussion depend on the underlying condition. Tell: dullness with decreased fremitus means fluid has collected, not inflammation alone.
